title: Pairs That Stay Equal After Reversal

concept.title: Rearrange the condition until each side depends on one number
body: Let `rev(x)` be `x` with its digits reversed (`rev(120) = 21`). A pair `i < j` is **nice** if `a[i] + rev(a[j]) = a[j] + rev(a[i])`. Move the terms around: `a[i] - rev(a[i]) = a[j] - rev(a[j])`. Now the left side depends only on `i` and the right side only on `j`: the pair is nice exactly when the two numbers have the **same value of `x - rev(x)`**.
Whenever a condition on two elements can be rewritten as "f(i) equals f(j)", a map of `f` values counts the pairs in one pass. The number of pairs can reach about 2 * 10^8, so use 64-bit integers.

statement: Let `rev(x)` be the number you get by writing the digits of `x` in the reverse order (for example `rev(120) = 21`). Count the pairs of positions `i < j` for which `a[i] + rev(a[j]) = a[j] + rev(a[i])`.

examples.note: x - rev(x) is 18 for 42, 0 for 11, 0 for 1 and 18 for 97, so the nice pairs are (42, 97) and (11, 1).

hints: Rearrange the equation so that each side depends on one number only.
The pair is nice when `x - rev(x)` is equal for both numbers.
Count equal keys with a map, adding the earlier count for each number.

solution.complexity: Time O(n * digits) on average, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

count = {}
total = 0
for x in a:
    key = x - int(str(x)[::-1])
    total += count.get(key, 0)
    count[key] = count.get(key, 0) + 1
print(total)
